Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, with Mirza Hussain Haider, Advocates — For the Appellants

full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: By this First Appeal, the plaintiff-appellant challenges the decisions of the trial Judge dismissing her suit for declaration of Title simpliciter over the property described in the schedule to the plaint. The suit was dismissed by the judgment dated September 19, 1987 followed by a decree of the Third Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka.

2. The portrayal of the essential facts forming the background of the appeal is set out thus:

The appellant as plaintiff on 11-12-1979 laid suit being Title Suit No. 893 of 1979 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which was, on transfer, re-numbered as Title Suit No. 574 of 1981 of the Third Court of Subordinate Judge in Dhaka. The subject matter of the suit appearing from the schedule to the plaint is 0.44 1/2 acres out of 0.89 acres of land on the northern portion of Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 under Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124 within Mouza-Brahman Chiran under Police Station Tejgaon now Motijheel, District-Dhaka, State Acquisition Plots being 471 entire and 473 portion.

3. Averments made in the plaint are that Cadestral Survey Plot No. 112 measuring an area of 0.53 and Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 measuring an area of 0.89 acres of Mouza-Brahman Chiran, Police Station-Tejgaon, District-Dhaka belonged to Sk Mainuddin who sold the same orally to Chand Bepari for a consideration of Taka 75.00. Chand Bepari breathed his last leaving behind, among others, two sons, Sultan Hossain and Abed Sheikh, two daughters Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi. Saburannessa Bibi, Johara Bibi and some other heirs of Chand Bepari instituted a Suit being Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 for partition of the property including the aforesaid two plots left by Chand Bepari against Sultan Hossain and others in the Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. In the said suit Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi got final decree and they took possession of the partitioned property through court. Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi sold their shares in several plots including the above stated two plots in favour of Kari Samiruddin Ahmed by a registered deed of conveyance dated 10-4-1922 who took over possession of the purchased land. Samiruddin, thereafter, on 30-5-1929 gifted half of the aforesaid plot Nos. 112 and 114 to Munshi Md Nowab Ali by a Deed of Gift dated 30-5-1929 and handed over the possession of the gifted property to the donee, Nowab Ali who subsequently transferred half of the Plot Nos. 112 and 114 to Sarama Sundari Guha by a registered Deed of Sale dated 5-1-1930. Sarama Sundari Guha got the northern portion of plot Nos. 112 and 114 by amicable partition among the co-sharers and, thereafter, sold the same to one Ramjan Ali by a registered Deed of Sale dated 8-12-1938. Ramjan Ali died leaving behind wife Faizun Nessa Bibi, 5 sons Abbas Ali, Ahmed Ali, Ansar, Abdur Razzak and Md Giasuddin and 2 daughters Amena Khatun and Sahara Khatun. 0.34 acres of land of plot No. 114 stood recorded in the name of Faizunnessa in State Acquisition Khatian Plot No. 473 and 0.37 acres of land of plot No. 114 was recorded in the name of Shamsuddin Mia who purchased from Asabuddin Mia and Abbasuddin Mia purchased from the heirs of Nowab Ali Mia and 0.18 acres of land of the said plot stood recorded in the name of the Province of East Pakistan in Khatian No. 1.

4. Further statements are that Faizunnessa and other heirs of Ramjan Ali transferred 0.311/2 acres of land to the plaintiff and 0.13 acres of land to Md Sona Mia from plot No. 114 by two separate registered sale deeds dated 16-2-1965 and the transferees were put into possession of the transferred land. Sona Mia, subsequently, transferred his 0.13 acres of land in favour of the plaintiff by a registered deed of sale dated 12-11-1966 and put later in possession of the same. The plaintiff, thus, in the manner stated above acquired title on 0.44 on 0.44½ acres of land in the northern portion of Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114. The plaintiff got her name recorded in the Record of Right in place of Faizunnessa with respect to 0.34 acres of land from the Revenue Officer and got 10½ acres of land recorded through civil Court in a proceeding under section 143A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The plaintiff paid rent with respect to the suit land upto the year 1383 BS The plaintiff has been all along in possession of the suit land since purchase and through labourers has been growing cauliflowers and paddy, etc. thereon. The defendants put forward claim on the suit land being the grand-sons and daughters of the Cadestral Survey recorded owner Mainuddin Sk who lost his interest on the suit land in the decree recorded in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916. The defendants got no right, title and interest in the suit land at any point of time. The wrong record of the suit land in the names of defendant Nos. 1-5 had cast cloud on the title of the plaintiff on the suit land and hence the suit. The cause of action of the suit arose on 20-11-1979 when the plaintiff came to know about the wrong record.

5. The defendant Nos. 10-18 being the transferees from the heirs of Abdul Halim, the defendant Nos. 1-5 had been added as defendants in the suit by way of an application under the provisions of Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The defendant Nos. 1-9 and defendant Nos. 10-17 presented two separate written statements traversing all the material allegations made in the plaint and also setting up their respective claims on the suit land.

6. Averments made in the written statement filed by the defendant Nos. 1-9 are that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner. The suit is barred by limitation and principles of waiver and estoppel. The suit is bad mis-joinder and non-joinder of parties. The suit land is vague and indefinite. The plaintiff nor her predecessors had ever been in possession of the suit land and the suit is hit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The suit property belonged to Sk Mainuddin whose name had been correctly recorded in the Cadestral Survey Record of Right and Sk Mainuddin had been possessing the suit property by constructing but and cultivating the land and enjoying the usufructs therefrom. Sk Mainuddin died leaving behind 2 sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Hali. There had been no partition suit amongst the co-sharers of Chand Bepari and no possession was taken of plot Nos. 112 and 114 through court by the Decree Holders. The Deed of Gift in favour of Md Nowab Ali and the subsequent transfer by Nawab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha in respect of 2 decimals of land of plot No. 114 is bogus. Ramzan Ali by purchase from Sarams Sundari Guha also did not acquire any title nor possession in the suit property. The suit property was all along vacant nal land and most of the year the same remained under water. The suit property had been in possession of the defendants since their fore-father and the same stood recorded in their names in State Acquisition and Revisional Settlement Khatian. Rents had been paid with respect to suit property. The defendants are the heirs and successors of Abdul Halim and Abdus Sattar who were the sons of Sk Mainuddin. Plaintiff got no right, title and interest in the suit land and the title deeds of the plaintiff are false, collusive and without consideration.

7. Statements made in the written statement of the defendant Nos. 10-17, in brief, are that the suit is not maintainable in its present form. The plaintiff got no cause of action for laying the suit. The plaintiff being completely out of possession of the suit property, the suit is not maintainable without the prayer for recovery of khas possession thereon on payment of ad valorem court fee according to the market value of the suit property. The suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The positive case set up by these defendants, is that in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 of the Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, Saburennessa Bibi and Johara Bibi, the alleged two daughters of Chand Bepari did not get the land of Cadestral Survey plot No 112 and 114 in their shaham nor did they get possession thereof through final decree. Saburennessa Bibi and Johara Bibi did not get any exclusive or separate Shaham for their share and the land of Cadestral Survey plot Nos. 112 and 114 never fell in their Shaham of the said partition suit. The deeds of transfer of the predecessors of the plaintiff are false, fictitious, collusive, fabricated documents and never acted upon and those were mere paper transactions. The predecessor transferees did never exercise any acts of possession on the suit plot No. 114. The alleged sale of northern half of Cadestral Survey plot Nos. 112 and 114 by Sarama Sundari Guha in favour of Ramjan Ali is a myth. The deed of transfer in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha dated 5-1-1930 was in respect of only 0.2 acres of land from Cadestral Survey plot No. 114. The two sale deeds dated 16-12-1965, one in favour of the plaintiff and the other in favour of Sona Mia are false, fictitious, collusive and fabricated documents and those were never acted upon and they were mere paper transactions.

8. Further pleading is, that Mainuddin Sk, who was also known as Mainuddin Kochoan, acquired the property of Cadestral Survey plot Nos. 114 and 112 from Sultan Hossain, son of Chand Bepari quite some time before the final publication of Cadestral Survey Record of Right and during the preparation of the said Record of Right, Mainuddin''''s name had been correctly recorded in CS Khatian No. 124. Out of the two Cadestral Survey plots, plot No. 112 with an area of 0.53 acres was the homestead of Mainuddin Sk and the other Cadestral Survey plot No. 114 having an area of 0.89 acres was nal land which always remained under deep water for several months during the rainy season and those remain unfit for cultivation for those months. Mainuddin Sk used to grow various kinds of vegetable during winter and dry season on the said plots. Mainuddin Sk having been in exclusive possession of the property of cadestral survey plot No. 114 died leaving behind two sons, Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim and the two brothers were in exclusive possession of the land of the said Cadestral Survey plot. Abdus Sattar died leaving behind his only son Abdul Mannan, defendant No. 6, Abdul Halim and Abdul Mannan were exercising acts of possession on the land of plot No. 114 by producing various kinds of vegetables after the recession of the rainy season. Abdul Halim died leaving behind one son Nurul Islam alias Nur Islam, defendant No. 1, three daughters Rezia Khatun, defendant No. 2, Tarana Begum defendant No. 3 and Hasina Begum defendant No. 5, and wife Begum Bibi defendant No. 4 and they used to exercise acts of possession on the land of plot No. 114 by growing paddy, various kinds of vegetable through Bargadars and hired labourers. The defendant Nos. 1-5, thereafter, having been in actual and physical possession of the land of Cadestral Survey plot No. 114 transferred land of the said plot in favour of the added defendant Nos. 10-17 for valuable consideration by several deeds of conveyance of different dates. The transferee defendant Nos. 10-17 are in actual possession of the land in respect of their respective shares in total denial of right, title and possession of all persons including the plaintiff. The particulars of the purchase of land by the defendant Nos. 10-17 have been given in a chart in the written statement. Clear assertion had been made by the defendants that the plaintiff never acquired any title to the suit property nor did she ever possess the land or any part thereof.

9. The plaintiff, thereafter, on 3-8-85 amended the plaint by way of an application under the provisions of Order 6 rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure and made a marked departure from the original stand taken by her at the time of presentation of the plaint in the court. The plaint after amendment stands as such:

"Chand Bepari died leaving behind two sons, Sultan Hossain and Abed Sk wife, Shahar Banoo Bibi @ Saker Bibi and five daughters Sayora, Saburonnessa, Johra Bibi, Marium and Rahamonnessa. Rahamonnessa died leaving behind her husband Abdul Gaffor and daughter Mayyara Bibi. After the death of Chand A   Bepari his eldest son Sultan Hossain sold the above plots to Mainuddin Kochwan and other lands to several other persons and Sultan Hossain sold much more than his inherited share. The other heirs of Chand Bepari, Sk Abed, his mother and sister including Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Khatoon & heirs of deceased sister brought Title Suit No.167 of 1916 for partition of all the properties left by Chand Bepari including CS Plot Nos. 112 and 114 of Brahman Chiran against Sultan Hossain and the purchasers from Sultan Hossain including Sk Mainuddin @ Mainuddin Kochwan who was defendant No. 21 of the said suit and Mainuddin Kochwan filed written statement in the said suit claiming the lands recorded in CS Plot Nos. 112 and 114 of Mouza Brahman Chiran and he died during the pendency of the suit. His heirs i.e. two sons Abdus Sattar and Azim @ Abdul Halim and wife Shaheron Bibi were substituted and the claim of the defendant No. 21 was disallowed by the learned Court. In the said suit, the plaintiffs including Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Khatoon got in their allotment the lands of CS Plot Nos. 112 and 114 and other properties and they got possession of their allotment through Court. The CS record of the said plots has, therefore, no legal force and validity".

10. In view of the amendment of the plaint the defendant Nos. 1-17 filed a joint additional written statement controverting the averments made in the amended plaint virtually reiterating the averments and stand taken by them in their original written statements.

11. The learned trial Judge framed four issues which are as follows:

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. Has the plaintiff right, title and interest in the suit property?

3. Is the plaintiff entitled to get the decree as prayed for?

4. To what other relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled?

12. Both the plaintiff and the defendants led evidence, both oral and documentary in support of the respective claims/contentions. A good number of documents had been exhibited from both the sides. Of course, many of the documents did not appear to have been proved and exhibited in accordance with the provisions of the Evidence Act. Some documents had been exhibited without any objection and some documents had been exhibited with objection.

13. 4 witnesses have been examined from the side of the plaintiff. 6 witnesses had been examined from the side of the defendant Nos. 10-17.

14. PW 1 Md Azim is the son of the plaintiff. He gave testimony that the suit land is mallard and the plaintiff has been in possession of the same by growing cauliflowers and pumpkin through Bargadar Abdur Razzak, PW 3. He further testified that for the last 2 years the suit land is under the possession of an appointed receiver. It is admitted by him that the suit land had been recorded in the name of the defendants in the Municipal Corporation. It is his further testimony that it had not been stated in the plaint that the plaintiff possessed the suit land through Bargadar. This witness denied the suggestion put forward from the side of the defendants that they did never possess the suit land and the defendants are in possession of the suit land.

15. PW 2 Siraj Mia in his evidence stated that the plaintiff cultivates the land through Reju Mia who is Abdur Razzak PW 3. The witness could not say who is the plaintiff of the suit.

16. PW 3 Abdur Razzak testified that there had been 5/7 old houses in the suit land. He stated that he has no plough or cows and he has been carrying on vegetable business and he opens his shop at 7-00 AM and closes at 10-00 PM and in that manner he has been running his vegetable business for the last 28 years. This witness denied the suggestion suggested from the defendant side that he never cultivated the suit land.

17. PW 4 Sona Mia gave testimony that PW 3 Abdur Razzak and his sons cultivated the suit land. This witness stated that there is no house in the suit land.

18. Defendant No. 16 is DW 1. This witness stated in his evidence that Mainuddin Sk was the owner of the suit land and the CS Record of Right stood is his name. He purchased 5 kathas of land from the suit property by way of three deeds of conveyance from the heirs of Abdul Halim. He got his name mutated in the connected Record of Right and paid rent and got Rent-Receipts. He constructed house on his share of the purchased land and the Municipal Holding stands in his name and he paid Municipal taxes to the authority concerned. He denied the suggestion put forward from the plaintiff side that his vendors had no title and possession over the suit land.

19. Defendant No. 15 is DW 2. His testimony is that Sk Mainuddin was the owner of the suit property and the CS Record of Right had been prepared in his name. Mainuddin Sk died leaving behind two sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim and he purchased 2 kathas and 5 chataks of land by virtue of two sale deeds from the heirs of Abdul Halim. He got his name mutated in the connected Record of Right and paid rents to the Government and got Rent Receipts. He also got his name mutated with the Municipality and Municipal Holding had been opened in his name and paid Holding Taxes. Further testimony is that the plaintiff did never exercise any acts of possession over the suit property.

20. Defendant No. 11 is DW 3. He gave evidence on his behalf and also on behalf of defendant No. 10 who is his wife. He gave evidence in the same line as given by DWs 1 and 2. He and his wife also purchased 11/2 kathas of land from the suit property from Tarana Begum, the heir of Abdul Halim. He and his wife got their names mutated in the connected Record of Right and separate Khatians had been opened in their names. He and his wife got names mutated in the Municipality and Municipal Holding had been opened in their names and they paid Municipal Taxes and got Tax Receipts. He testified that the plaintiff did never exercise any acts of possession on the suit property.

21. The defendant No. 17 is DW 4. He and his wife Nurjahan Begum purchased 2 kathas of land from Begum Bibi, the heir of Abdul Halim. The testimony is, that they got their names mutated in the connected Record of Right and paid rents and got Rent Receipts. They also got their names mutated in the Municipality and Holding had been opened in their names and Municipality taxes were paid in their names.

22. DW 5 is Sura Zamal. He is the owner of the land contiguous to the suit property. He stated that the suit property is the contiguous western plot of his property. He saw Abdul Halim and Abdus Sattar, the sons of Mainuddin Sk to exercise acts of possession on the suit property and on their death their heirs possessed the land by growing pumpkin, dates and other vegetables. He testified that no other person except the defendants possessed the land.

23. DW 6 is the son of defendant No. 9, the heir of Abdus Sattar. He gave testimony that the defendant Nos. 6-9 possessed the southern portion of the suit plot. Dr Abul Bashar and others (defendant Nos. 10-17) possessed the northern portion of the suit property. This witness testified that he obtained the certified copy of the kabala deed executed by Nawab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari and in schedule No. 6 of the deed, the plot No. was stated as 124 and there is reference of transfer of 2 decimals of land and in place of plot No. 124, 114 had been inserted by act of interpolation. This witness in cross-examination stated that plot Nos. 112 and 114 had been recorded in the name of Abdul Halim and others in State Acquisition Survey Operation.

24. The learned trial Judge decided Issue No. 1 against the plaintiff. In arriving at the decision, he appears to have considered the oral evidences of witnesses of the plaintiff as well as the documentary evidences. He found glaring contradictions in the testimonies of PWs 1, 2 and 3. He also considered the evidences of the defendants, both oral and documentary, the Report of the Badar Amin, Exhibit G showing possession of the defendants over the suit property, Mutation and the Corrected Record of Right in the names of the defendants, Municipal Holding, Rent Receipts and Municipal Tax Receipts showing payment of rent and Municipal taxes to the authority concerned. On an analysis of all the legal evidences brought on record he recorded the finding that the plaintiff did never possess the suit property and the suit is hit under proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act since the plaintiff did not pray for recovery of possession by way of consequential relief and the suit is not maintainable.

25. The learned trial Judge also decided issue No. 2 against the plaintiff. In deciding the said issue the learned Judge recorded the following findings:

a) From the certified copy of the Decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916, Exhibit 1 it appeared that there were 8 schedules of land from Ka to Jha. Description of the land in Exhibit 1 had been shown by boundary and it was not possible to ascertain whether the schedule of Exhibit 1 attracted the suit plot No. 114. The plaintiff also did not state in her plaint as to which of the schedules of Exhibit 1 was the suit land and there was also no attempt from the side of the plaintiff to prove which of the schedules of Exhibit 1 was the suit land. PW 1 in his cross-examination stated that he could not say who got which plot of land.

b) From Exhibit 2 series (Final Decree, Field Book, Map, etc. of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916) it appeared that Advocate Commissioner in his Field Book had shown one Abdus Sattar in possession of the schedule Cha and Ta (ত) land of that partition suit and since the plaintiff failed to show that the said decree was executed within 12 years it could not be presumed that Abdus Sattar was dispossessed from the possession as found by the Advocate Commissioner.

c) No rebuttable evidence could be adduced by the plaintiff to show that Cadestral Survey Khatian was wrongly prepared which, in fact, got presumptive value.

d) From Exhibit I it appeared that one Mainuddin Kochwan was defendant No. 21 and after his death his two sons, namely, Abdus Sattar and Azim (minors) were substituted as defendant Nos. 21 Kha and 21 Ga and minor Azim was shown to have been represented by his minor brother Abdus Sattar as guardian and the plaintiff failed to show that as per Order XXXI, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, court guardian was appointed by the court to represent the interest of the said minor defendants.

e) From the certified copy of the sale deed by Munshi Nowab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha it appeared that Nowab Ali sold 2 decimals of land of CS plot No. 124 under khatian No. 124 and on close scrutiny it appeared that CS plot No. 124 was made as 114 by over writing with a view to tally the same with the suit plot No. 114. From Exhibit-6 it appeared that Sarama Sundari Guha sold 0.44½ acres of land of CS plot No. 114 whereas it appeared from the schedule No. 6 of Exhibit 5 that Sarama Sundari Guha purchased only 0.02 decimals of land of CS plot No. 124 and, thus, Sarama Sundari Guha could not sell 0.44½ acres of land to Ramjan Al and the legal heirs of Ramjan Ali could not transfer. 0.331/2 acres of land to the plaintiff and 0.13 acres of land to Sona Mia by Exhibits 7 and 8 respectively.

f) Exhibit 10 is the certified copy of Mutated Khatian in favour of the plaintiff for 0.101/2 acres of land but no order of the Mutation Case was filed to show whether the defendant Nos. 1-9 who are legal heirs of the CS recorded owner Sk Mainuddin were parties in that proceeding.

g) Exhibit 13 is the Dakhila alleged to have been granted by the Superior Landlord in favour of Ramjan Ali but no attempt was made by the plaintiff to call for counter-foil of Rent Receipt and no witness was produced to prove the said Rent Receipt and the Record of Right and payment of rent, do not confer any title.

26. In the light of the decisions arrived at by the learned trial Judge on issue Nos. 1, 2, issue Nos. 3 and 4 were also decided against the plaintiff. Recording the above decisions, the trial Judge dismissed the suit.

27. The plaintiff having felt aggrieved of such adjudication of the trial judge, sought setting aside the judgment and the decree followed from it, through a medium of appeal before this Court.

28. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mr Mirza Hussain Haider, learned Advocates appeared in support of the appeal. The contesting respondent Nos. 15 and 16 have been represented by the learned Advocate Mr Md Moksudur Rahman, with Mr Md Fazlul Karim, Mr Md Mazibar Rahman, Mr Khondaker Modarresh Elahi and Mr MA Mannan Mohan, the learned Advocates.

29. The arguments have occupied as many as 7 days and they have ranged over a good number of issues and points. Written submissions had been also presented before us. Some authorities both of our jurisdiction and Indian Jurisdiction have been brought to our attention.

30. Contentions pressed into service from the side of the plaintiff-appellant are as follows:

i)	Since the suit was for declaration of title over the suit property, the court was to decide first whether the plaintiff got title on the suit property. Title of the plaintiff had been traced from the Final decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 of the Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka over the properties especially Cha and The (3) property detailed in the schedule to the plaint in favour of the plaintiffs of the said Suit including Saburennessa and Johara Bibi, plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 of the suit, daughters of Chand Bepari and the claim of Mainuddin Kochwan, the defendant No. 21 of the said suit on Cha and The (TO property stood rejected and the plaintiff by virtue of the subsequent Transfer from the Decree-Holders Saburennessa and Johora Bibi stepped into their shoes and the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error in holding that the plaintiff got no title on the suitland.

ii)	The plaintiff, along with the title, could successfully prove her possession on the suit property from the period of their predecessor, the Decree-Holders of the previous Title Suit and the Court failed to assess the legal evidence adduced from the side of the plaintiff on the factum of possession and thus committed a substantial error in recording the finding that the plaintiff failed to prove her possession on the suit land and the suit is hit by proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for not seeking consequential relief in the form of recovery of khash possession over the suit property.

iii) The presumption attached to the SC Record of Right in the name of Mainuddin Kochwan had been successfully rebutted by the plaintiff and Decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 is a rebuttable piece of evidence and the court fell into an error in holding that no rebuttable evidence could be adduced by the plaintiff to show that CS Khatian was wrongly prepared and the CS Khatian got a presumptive value.

31. Contentions, on the other hand, advanced from the side of the defendant-respondents are catalogued hereunder:

i) The plaintiff through legal evidence signally failed to prove title and possession over the suit property and the judgment under challenge is well-founded both on law and fact and, as such, no interference is called for by this Court in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction.

ii) From the certified copy of the Decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 it is not at all possible to ascertain whether. Exhibit 1 attracted suit plot No. 114, description of which had been given by boundary. Plaintiff also did not state in the plaint of the instant suit as to which of the schedules of the Decree was the suit land and there was no attempt from the side of the plaintiff-appellant to prove which of the schedules of the Decree, Exhibit 1, was the suit land and, thus, CS plot No. 114 cannot be said to have fallen in the shares of Saburennessa and Johora Bibi, the daughters of Chand Bepari and the plaintiff cannot trace her title to CS Plot No. 114.

iii) There is nothing on record to show that the Decree in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 was executed within 12 years of the Decree as provided in section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the said decree is of no avail to the plaintiff. In support of the said contention, Md Abdur Rahim and others vs Sree Sree Gredhari Jeo, 27 DLR 72 and ADC (Revenue) Pabna vs Md Abdul Halim Mia, 48 DLR (AD) 141 has been referred to.

iv) In the previous Title Suit No. 167 of 1916, the substituted defendant Nos. 21 Kha and 21 Ga were minors and the minor substituted respondent No. 21 Ga Abdul Hakim had been shown to have been represented by his minor brother defendant No. 21 Kha Abdus Sattar and the said minor defendant was not even represented duly by an appointed guardian and the decree against him is void and inoperative in law and the same cannot be enforced against them. Support for this contention has been sought to be drawn in Ram Chandra Arya vs Man Singh and another, AIR 1968 SC 954.

v) Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 abated as a whole in the absence of due substitution of the heirs of deceased defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sk and abatement is an automatic process and does not require any formal order of the court. Province of East Pakistan vs Haji Muslimullah and others, 29 DLR 762, Wall and others vs Manish Ali and others, 17 DLR (SC) 536, Master Abdul Aziz vs Abani Mohan Mukherjee and others, 30 DLR (SC) 221 and Shefar Alam Nizamee vs Mrs Karima Begum Haridunnessa and others, 40 DLR 422 has been referred to for the said contention.

vi) The presumption attached to the Cadestral Survey Record of Right in the name of Mainuddin Sk could not be at all rebutted by any evidence and in the absence of any rebuttable evidence there will be presumption of the correctness of the said Record of Right in the name of Sk Mainuddin. Authorities such as Alauddin Munshi and others vs Mainuddin Talukder and others, 14 DLR 725, Jalal Ahmed Choudhury vs Azizur Rahman and others, 17 DLR 340, Pramatha Nath Choudhury and 17 others vs Kamir Mondal, 17 DLR (SC) 392 and Akrab Ali and others vs Zahiruddin Kari and others, 30 DLR (SC) 81 has been relied upon in support of the said contention.

vii) In the Sale deed executed by Nowab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundoi Guha, Exhibit 5, there is overwriting of plot No. 114 in place of plot No. 124 and the land transferred by the said sale deed is 0.02 acres of land and the chain of devolution of interest given by the plaintiff is, thus, broken and it goes against the plaint case and the learned Subordinate Judge correctly found that Munshi actually sold 0.02 acres of land from CS plot No. 124 and since the chain of devolution of interest and title has been disrupted at the stage of Exhibits 4 and 5, plaintiff cannot acquire title on the basis of alleged title allegedly acquired by Sarama Sundari Guha and others.

viii) From Exhibit 2 series (Final decree, Field Book, Map etc.) of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 it appeared that Advocate Commissioner in his Field Book had shown one Abdus Sattar in possession of Schedule Cha and Tha (3) land of the said suit and since the plaintiff failed to show that the said decree was executed within 12 years, it cannot be presumed that Abdus Sattar who was found in possession of schedule Cha and Tha (3) land was dispossessed.

ix) No cause of action has been disclosed by the plaintiff in the plaint and the mere knowledge of the alleged wrong record cannot be a cause of action without making any allegation against any act of the defendants giving rise to cause of action and no evidence has been adduced by the plaintiff for proving the cause of action which is the alleged knowledge of the plaintiff as to the wrong record of the suit property. Reliance has been put in support of the contention raised on Ram Awalamb and others vs Jata Sankar and others, AIR 1969 Allahabad 526 (FB).

x) The suit is bad for defect of parties for not impleading the Government as defendant which is necessary as provided in Article 6(vi) of President Order No. 142 of 1972.

32. In the wake of rival contentions advanced from both the sides, we will now address ourselves to examine the merit of the contentions so raised.

33. In approaching the appeal and before examination of the merit of the contentions it needs taking notice that in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916, the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hussain was the son of Chand Bepari who was the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs of the stated suit including plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 Saburennessa Bibi and Johra Bibi who are the predecessor-in-interest of the present plaintiff. The defendant Nos. 2-30 including the defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan were transferees from defendant No. 1 Sultan Hussain. Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim were the two sons of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan and Abdul Halim is the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant Nos. 1-5. The defendant Nos. 10-17 are transferees from defendant Nos. 1-5. <u>37. Burden of proof is the obligation to adduce evidence to the satisfaction of the court in order to establish the existence or non-existence of a fact contended by a party. This Rule is derived from the Roman Law and is supportable not only on the ground of fairness but also upon that of the greater practical difficulty which is involved in proving a negative than in proving an affirmative. This Rule is an ancient Rule founded on consideration of good sense and should not be departed from without strong reasons.</u>

<u>45. We now turn to a vital contention addressed before us on behalf of the defendant-appellant which is, that Mainuddin Kochwan, the defendant No. 21 of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 having been dead during the pendency of the suit, his heirs, two minor sons. Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim, were not, properly and legally substituted and the minor Abdul Halim had been shown to have been represented by his another minor brother Abdus Sattar and no court guardian as required under the provision of Order XXXII rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure had been at all appointed and, as such, the decree against the said two minor defendants without having been properly represented by a court guardian is void and inoperative and the decree so passed was not binding upon them. The said contention has been attempted to be controverted by the plaintiff-appellant raising the plea that in the written statement filed by the defendants nowhere there is an averment that Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim, the two sons of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan, were minors.</u>

<u>46. Before adverting to the contentions raised fi urn both tfae sides it will be useful to notice the relevant provision of law.</u>

<u>47. Suits by or against minors and persons of unsound mind are contained in Order XXXII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

<u>Order XXXII rule 3 is extracted hereunder:</u>

<u>"3. (1) Where the defendant is a minor, the Court, on being satisfied of the fact of his minority, shall appoint a proper person to be guardian for the suit for such minor.</u>

<u>(2) An order for the appointment of a guardian for the suit may be obtained upon application in the name and on behalf of the minor or by the plaintiff.</u>

<u>(3) Such application shall be supported by an affidavit verifying the fact that the proposed guardian has no interest in the matters in controversy in the suit adverse to that of the minor and that he is a fit person to be so appointed.</u>

<u>(4) No order shall be made on any application under this rule except upon notice to the minor and to any guardian of the minor appointed or declared by an authority competent in that behalf, or, where there is no such guardian, upon notice to the father or other natural guardian, to the person in whose care the minor is and after hearing any objection which may be urged on behalf of any person served with notice under this sub-rule.</u>

<u>(5) A person appointed under sub-rule (1) to be guardian for the suit for a minor shall, unless his appointment is terminated by retirement, removal or death, continue as such throughout all proceedings arising out of the suit including proceedings in any appellate or revisional Court and any proceedings in the execution of a decree."</u>

<u>48. Order XXXII rule 3 enjoins that where the defendant is a minor the court on being satisfied of the fact of his minority, shall appoint a proper person to be guardian for the suit for such minor. In Rule 3 the word "shall" is construed to be mandatory and not directory. The above provision manifests that a minor is to be represented by a proper person as his guardian in the civil proceedings through the trial, appeal or revision and in no case he would be unrepresented or to be placed ex parte for the one reason or the other. The appointment of a guardian, therefore, of minor heirs of defendant who died during pendency of suit is absolutely necessary. A minor cannot be considered to be a party to suit unless he is properly represented in a suit by a duly qualified and competent guardian. When a minor has legally become a party to the suit, only then the court would acquire jurisdiction to decide the case. Decree passed against an unrepresented minor defendant being a decree against a person not a party to the suit would be without jurisdiction, null and void. In other words, it can be said that a decree passed against a minor defendant not properly represented is without jurisdiction and a nullity.</u>

<u>49. Keeping in view the principles of law indicated above let us deal with the substantial point so debated. Defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 died during the pendency of the Suit leaving behind one wife Sahana Bibi, and two minor sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Azim alias Abdul Halim respectively. The said heir wife Sahani Bibi had been substituted by the plaintiff as defendant No. 21 Ka and the two minor heir sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim had been substituted as defendant No. 21 Kha and 21Ga. The minor defendant No. 21 Ga Abdul Halim had been shown to have been represented by his minor brother substituted defendant No. 21 Kha Abdus Sattar. The defendant No. 21 Kha Abdus Sattar being a minor was absolutely incompetent to represent his minor brother Abdul Halim, the defendant No. 21Ga. The plaintiffs of the previous suit fraudulently had shown minor defendant No. 21Ga Abdul Halim to have been represented by another minor brother the defendant No. 21 Kha. On perusal of Exhibit I and Exhibit 2 series it transpires that in the plaint, the Preliminary Decree and the Final Decree, the substituted defendant Nos. 21 Kha and 21Ga had been described as minors and they were not at all represented by any guardian appointed by the court as mandated under Order XXXII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Their address were not shown. The suit was decreed ex parte against the minor defendant Nos. 21 Kha. The decree passed in the suit against them being totally unrepresented by a guardian appointed by the court was wholly without jurisdiction and the same was a nullity. The said decree having been without jurisdiction and nullity could not and cannot be enforced against them and also against the present defendant No.1-9 who are their heirs and also the transferee defendant Nos. 10-17. In Ram Chandra Arya vs Man Singh and others, AIR 1968 (SC) 954 relied on from the side of the defendant-respondents, a decree against one Ramlal, a lunatic had been passed in contravention of the provisions of Order XXXII, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure and a Sale had been held in execution of the said decree. The Lunatic was not represented by a guardian appointed by the court. The Supreme Court of India stated thus: It is now well settled principle that, if a decree is passed against a minor without appointment of guardian, the decree is a nullity and is void and not merely voidable. This principle becomes applicable to the case of a lunatic in view of rule 15 of Order 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The decree has A) be treated as without jurisdiction and the Sale deed in execution of that decree also be held to be void: We are in respectful agreement with the proposition of law stated in the said authority.</u>

<u>50. Some other authorizes on the subject may also, be, noticed. The board principle that there cannot be any decree against persons not properly represented  the record was laid down by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council as far back as in 1904 in Khairajmal vs Dain, 32 Indian Appeal 23 PC. It was observed that if any decree is passed against a person not properly represented, the decree became a "nullity" and may be disregarded without any proceeding to set that aside. This principle was elaborate) as regards a minor defendant in the later case of Rashidunnessa vs Md Ismail, 36 Indian Appeal 168 PC holding that a decree against a minor would be a nullity where</u>

<u>(i) no guardian ad-litem is appointed.</u>

<u>(ii) no proper person is appointed. In Nirmal Chandra Roy and others vs Khandu Gosh and others, AIR 1952 Calcutta 562 the observation is couched in the following language : The provisions of sub-rule (4) of rule 3 and sub-rule (3) of rule 4 of Order 32 are mandatory and a decree obtained against a minor in complete disregard of the provision is without jurisdiction and void ab-initio: In Sheikh Abdul Karim vs Thakur Das Thakur and others, AIR 1928 Calcutta 844, Rankin CJ stated that Decree without appointment of guardian ad-)item of a minor in a suit against him being quite incumbent is a nullity against him. In Gobinda Prasad and another vs Shanti Swarup and others, AIR 1935 Allahabad 778 a Division Bench consisting of Jhon and Iqbal Ahmed JJ observed thus: The provisions of Order 32 Rule 3 that where the defendant is a minor, the court on being satisfied of the fact of his minority shall appoint a proper person to be guardian for the suit, are mandatory. A decree passed against a minor without appointment of a guardian-ad-litem is a nullity: In Saadullah Khan and others vs Kakijan and others, PLD 1962 Peshawar 117 it has been ruled by the Peshawar High Court that it is well established principle of law that a decree passed against a minor, who was not duly represented has no binding force against him.</u>

<u>51. We now propose to meet the plea taken from the side of the plaintiff-appellant that in the written statement filed by the defendants, nowhere there is any statement that Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim, the two sons of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan, were minors. <u>52. The learned Trial Judge noticed and considered this vital aspect of the case and also kept in view the provision of law as mandated under Order XXXII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and recorded the correct decision on this question.</u>

<u>53. Keeping in view the facts, circumstances, materials on record and the principles of law we are of this positive view that the decree passed against the minor defendant Nos. 21 Kha and 21Ga, Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim of the said suit is a nullity and the said decree is not binding upon them and the same is also not enforceable against them. We are also, of the further view that the said decree is not binding and not enforceable against the heirs and successive heirs of Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim, the defendant Nos. 1- 9 and also against the defendant Nos. 10-17 who stepped into their shoes by way of purchase through several deeds of conveyance and the said decree is of no assistance to the present plaintiff against the defendants.</u>

58. 59. The defendant No. 16 is DW 1. Defendant No. 15 is DW 2. Defendant No. 11 is DW 3. The wife of DW 3 is defendant No. 10. The defendant No.17 is DW 4. DW 5 is a witness on factum of possession. <u>60. The learned trial Judge on a proper discussion and consideration of the evidences and materials brought on record correctly recorded the decision that the plaintiff failed to prove her title on the suit land and also failed to prove possession and the plaintiff having not prayed for the relief of recovery of khas possession on the suit property, the suit is not maintainable as being hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. We, on a careful perusal of the pleadings of the respective parties, a discreet analysis of the legal evidences both oral and documentary and also taking into consideration all the materials brought on record, are of this considered view that the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff had no possession on the suit property and the plaintiff also got no possession thereon and the predecessor-in-interest of the defendants Nos. 1-9 had been although in possession of the suit property and the defendant Nos. 1-9 exercised acts of possession thereon and the defendant Nos. 10-17 having stepped into the shoes of the defendant Nos. 1-9 by way of purchase are in possession of the suit property.</u>

<u>61. We now turn to the submission advanced on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant that the presumption attached to the Cadestral Survey Record of Right in the name of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan stood rebutted by legal evidence from the side of the plaintiff-appellant and the decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 is a rebuttable piece of evidence.</u>

<u>62. For the purpose of appreciating the soundness of the contention raised, the provisions of section 103(B)(5) of Bengal Tenancy Act may be noticed. Section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act enjoins that every entry in a Record of Right finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect.</u>

<u>63. Cadastral Survey Record of Right is the oldest Record of Right in our country. Onus of proving that Cadestral Survey Record of Right is wrong is on the person who alleges it. The plaintiff-appellant challenged the correctness of the Cadestral Survey Record of Right and so onus is definitely upon the plaintiff to show that entry in the Record of Right as prepared under section 103 (B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is wrong. In Aminuddin Biswas vs Miajan Biswas, 12 DLR 103 it has been held: The presumption of correctness as available on the strength of section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act has got to be rebutted by the person who alleges it : In this context it needs be stated that where a person relies upon the entry in the Record of Right for the basis of his title he is not required to show the basis of the entry in the Record of Right. It is also to be noted that the presumption attached to the Cadestral Record of Right prepared under section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is not rebutted on the reason that there is no evidence for the basis of the entry. In Alauddin Munshi and others vs Mainuddin Talukder and others, 14 DLR 725 it has been posited: Merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of right, the presumption is not rebutted in view of the provision of the Bengal Tenancy Act and also the procedure laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the officer concerned while preparing the final records of rights. There must be further evidence to show that the evidences are incorrect : In Akrab Ali and others vs Zahiruddin Karia and others, 30 DLR (SC) 81, the presumption of the correctness of an entry in the Record of Right has been considered. It has been laid down by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court that according to section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act every entry in the Record of Right finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. It had already been pointed out that in the plaint of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 in paragraph 4 there is clear averment that the defendant No.1 Sultan Hossain and the defendants 2-30 who are the transferees from defendant No.1 were in possession of the entire suit property detailed in the schedule of the said suit. The learned Advocate Commissioner found Abdus Sattar in possession of Schedule Cha and Tha (3) land and in the Field Book he noted the possession of Abdus Sattar on the said Cha and Tha (3) land. There is no evidence that the decree of partition Suit had been executed on evicting the defendants especially the heirs of defendant No. 21, Abdus Sattar and the Decree-Holder plaintiffs specially plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 of the said suit, Saburennessa and Johara Bibi got into possession of the decreed land. The Cadestral Survey Record of Right was finally published in the district of Dhaka round about the year 1929, perhaps before the amendment of Bengal Tenancy Act in 1929. The plaintiff has not adduced any evidence at all what was the state of possession of the suit land at the time of preparation of Cadestral Survey Record of Right. The decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 having not been executed at all, the said decree cannot be said to be a rebuttable piece of evidence rebutting the presumption of the correctness of the Cadestral Survey Record of Right standing in the name of Mainuddin Sheikh alias Mainuddin Kochwan. The presumption of the correctness of the entry in the Cadestral Survey Record of Right does not appear to have been rebutted by the plaintiff-appellant. The learned trial Judge on consideration of the legal evidences and materials on record recorded the finding that no rebuttable evidence could be adduced by the plaintiff to show that CS Khatian was wrongly prepared which, in fact, got presumptive value. No exception can be taken to the said decision arrived at by the trial Judge.</u>

64. Then comes the argument put forward on behalf of the defendant-respondents that the Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 abated as a whole in the absence of due substitution of the heirs of deceased defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheik alias Mainuddin Kochwan and abatement does not require any formal order of the court and the same is automatic. The argument is absolutely misconceived and not tenable in law.

65. It cannot be said that there was no substitution of the heirs of deceased defendant No.21 Mainuddin Sheikh. The heirs of deceased defendant No. 21 including his two minor sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim were very much substituted in the suit as substituted defendant No. 21 Kha and 21 Ga. The legal predicament which occurred in the substitution can be said that since they were minors they were required to be represented by a guardian appointed by the court as mandated under Order XXXII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But no guardian ad-interim had been appointed for them by the court. So, the question is not of non-substitution, rather the same is the proper representation of the two minor substituted defendants, Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim. The question of recording an order of abatement in that Title Suit, therefore, cannot at all arise in the present suit and this court in adjudication of the present Title Suit also got no jurisdiction to record any order for abatement of the said Title suit wherein Final decree had been passed in the year 1920. Some precedents has been placed before us on the point of abatement of the suit but we do not intend to make an idle parade of discussing those precedents as none of those are relevant on the subject matter and got no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case before us. It is to be borne in mind that each and every judgment must be read as applicable to the particular facts proved or assumed and the generality of the expressions used must be read as qualified by the particular facts of the case and the issues raised therein. The contention so rose having been absolutely misconceived and devoid of any substance, thus, fails.

<u>66. The other question debated on behalf of the defendant-respondents now remains to be answered. The question is non-disclosure of any cause of action in the Suit. Objection on the cause of action is pressed taking the plea that mere knowledge of the alleged wrong record cannot be a cause of action without making any allegation against any act of the defendants giving rise to cause of action.</u>

<u>67. The term "cause of action" has not been defined in the Code of Civil Procedure nor in any other Statute. "Cause of action" defined in Wharton''''s Law Lexicon, Fourteenth Edition, is as follows:</u>

<u>All the facts which are necessary to establish the plaintiff''''s right to the remedy what he claims.</u>

<u>"Cause of action" stated in Black''''s Law Dictionary is as hereunder:</u>

<u>"The facts or facts which give a person a right to judicial redress or relief against another. The legal effect of an occurrence in terms of redress to a party to the occurrence. A situation or state of facts which would entitle party to sustain action and give him right to seek a judicial remedy in his behalf. Fact, or a state of facts, to which law sought to be enforced against a person or thing applies. Facts which give to one or more relations of right-duty between two or more persons. Matter for which action may be maintained. Unlawful violation or invasion of right. The right which a party has to institute a judicial proceeding".</u>

<u>68. The meaning of "cause of action" which has been considered in numerous cases can be traced back to the case of Cook vs Gill, (1873) 8 CP 107: 28 LT 32 (H) from which it was quoted with approval by Lord Esher MR in Read vs Brown, (1888) 22 QBD 128 (1) According to that definition the term means.</u>

<u>"every fact which it would be necessary for the plaintiff to prove, if traversed, in order to support his right to the judgment of the court, but does not comprise every piece of evidence which is necessary to be proved."</u>

<u>A Full Bench of Allahabad High Court in Murti vs Bhola Ram, ILR 16 All 165 (f) interpreted the term as meaning</u>

<u>"the whole bundle of material and essential facts which it is necessary for the plaintiff to prove in order to entitle him to succeed in the suit".</u>

<u>In Mt Chand Koer vs Pratab Singh, 15 Ind App 156 (K) the Privy Council laid down that "the cause of action refers to the media upon which the plaintiff asks the court to arrive at a conclusion in his favour".</u>

<u>After observing</u>

<u>"Now the cause of action has no relation whatever to the defence which might be set up by the defendants, nor does it depend upon the character of the relief prayed for the plaintiff''''.</u>

<u>69. Regarding the meaning of this expression the matter is concluded by the dictum of the Privy Council in Md Khalil vs Mahbub Ali AIR 1949 PC 78, where this expression was examined in connection with its meaning under Order II, rule 2, CPC After an elaborate discussion of the authorities prevailing in Indian and English Law their Lordships summed up the principles in paragraph 61 of the judgment as follows:</u>

<u>"61. …………</u>

<u>(1) The correct test in cases falling under Order II, rule 2, is whether the claim in the new suit is, in fact, founded upon a cause of action distinct from that which was the foundation of the former suit''''. (Moonshee Buzloor Ruheem vs Shumsoonnissa Begum, (1887)11 Moo IA 551:2 Sar 259 (PC).</u>

<u>(2) The 'cause of action' means every fact which will be necessary for the plaintiff to prove if traversed in order to support his right to the judgment. (Read vs Brown, (1889) 22 QBD 128 : 58 LJQB 1201).</u>

<u>(3) If the evidence to support the two claims is different. (Brunsden vs Humphrey, (1884) 14 QBD 141: 53 LJQB 476).</u>

<u>(4) The causes of action in the two suits may be considered to be same if in substance they are identical. (Brunsden vs Humphrey, supra).</u>

<u>(5) The causes of action has no relation whatever to the defence that may be set up by the defendant nor does it depend upon the character of the relief prayed for the plaintiff. It refers to media upon which the plaintiff asks the Court to arrive at a conclusion in his favour. (Mt Chandkour vs Partab Singh, (1887)15 IA 156: ILR 16 C 98 (PC). This observation was made by Lord Watson in a case under section 43 of the Act of 1882 (corresponding to Order II, rule 2) where plaintiff made various claims in the same".</u>

<u>70. The expression "cause of action", thus, means the entire bundle of facts which a plaintiff has to prove in order to be eligible for the grant of relief. In other words, it can be stated that the facts that are alleged in the plaint and which are required to be proved without proof of which the plaintiff would not be entitled to a judgment, constitute the cause of action. Equally it can be said that a cause of action presupposes the existence of a right in the plaintiff which right has either been infringed or is threatened to be infringed. The right must be a substantive right, or it may pertain only to procedure, but the right must be there. Whether any particular facts constitute a cause of action has to be determined with reference to the facts of each case and with reference to the substance rather than the form of the action. Cause of action cannot be construed in an isolated way and the whole averments made in the plaint are to be seen and taken together to see whether any cause of action has been disclosed or not. It is the plaint as a whole which is to be construed and not the terminology or for that matter, a few stray references.</u>

<u>71. Bearing the principles stated above we have to approach the controversy which is whether cause of action has been disclosed in the plaint. True it is that there is no averment in the plaint that the Title of the plaintiff on the suit property had been invaded by the defendants giving an immediate action for laying the suit before the court. The cause of action of the suit had been alleged from the knowledge of the Record of Right in the name of the defendants. It is also true that there occurred some fundamental defects and infirmities in the plaint. But it cannot be suggested that the plaint did not consist of material facts giving rise to a cause of action for the plaintiff to lay the suit in the court. In Ram Awalamb and others vs Jata Sankar and others, AIR 1969 Allahabad 526 (F13) relied upon on behalf of the defendant-respondents, the principle of law is that in each and every case the cause of action of the suit shall have to be scrutinized to determine whether the suit is solely cognizable by a revenue court or is impliedly cognizable only by a revenue court or is cognizable by a civil Court. The said case is of no assistance to the defendant-respondent inasmuch as the facts of the present case are altogether different from the facts of the said case and law laid therein is also inapplicable. The contention that the plaint did not disclose a cause of action appears to be meritless and the same stands rejected.</u>

<u>72. The last contention addressed before us from the side of the defendant-respondents that the suit is bad for defect of parties for not impleading the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in the suit as mandated in Article 6(6) of President's Order No. 142 of 1972 now remains to be considered.</u>

<u>73. For appreciating the contention raised, the Preamble of President''s Order No. 142 of 1972 which is called the Bangladesh Transfer of Immovable Property (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 and Article 6 of the said Order may be conveniently looked into which are extracted hereunder:</u>

<u>Preamble: Whereas it is expedient to make provisions for restricting the transfer of immovable property in Bangladesh in public interest;</u>

<u>The Article 6 of the said Order is to the following effect:</u>

<u>Article 6: No person shall without joining the Government which shall be a necessary party, file or proceed with any suit.</u>

<u>(a) For the specific performance of any contract relating to the transfer of any immovable property or for declaration of title to or assertion of ownership of any such property.</u>

<u>(b) For enforcement of mortgage security in relation to any immovable property except where the mortgage is the movement or a local authority or a schedule Bank or a statutory Corporation or a Co-operative Society or</u>

<u>(c) For partition of immovable property where total area of the property involved exceeds one hundred standard bighas.</u>

<u>74. The question now comes whether the suit for declaration of Title as is contemplated in clause (a), of Article 6 is the kind of suit out of which the present appeal arises.</u>

<u>75. Keeping the dominant purpose of the enactment in view it is evidently clear that the words "any such property" as used in clause (a) of the Article will not be referable to any immovable property, but to any immovable property which is the subject matter of a contract relating to transfer. We are of this considered view that the provision of Article 6 of the President Order No. 142 of 1972 has no manner of application in a Suit for declaration of title like the present one and the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, as such, is not at all necessary party and the suit cannot fail in not impleading the Government of Bangladesh as defendant. The contention raised from the side of the defendant-respondents being without any substance, fails.</u>

76. We now propose to direct our attention to one legal aspect which is admissibility of documents as Exhibits. Many of the documents produced by the plaintiff were not admitted into evidence and exhibited in accordance with the provisions contained in the Evidence Act. A good number of documents has been exhibited with the certified copies. Exhibits 3, 4, 5 and 6 are all certified copies of the original documents and those copies were not even of 30 years old. The certified copies of those documents were obtained on 15-10-1979, 15-12-1978, 4-12-78 and 7-7-1979. The suit was registered on 11-12-1979. The certified copies of those documents i.e. the Deeds of Transfer were not admitted into evidence and exhibited in fulfilment of the requirement of law mandated in the Evidence Act. Exhibit 13 is a Rent Receipt allegedly granted by the Superior Landlord in favour of Ramjan Ali, the Vendor of the plaintiff and the said Rent Receipt is definitely a private document which was required to be proved in accordance with law but that was not so in this particular case.

<u>77. We shall now address ourselves to the application filed by the plaintiff-appellant under the provisions of Order XLI rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The plaintiff-appellant by the said application wants to get admitted as additional evidence two documents, Annexure 'A' and 'B'. The defendant-respondents by presenting an Affidavit-in-opposition resisted the said application contending that the documents attempted to be admitted as additional evidence will not be helpful in the pronouncement of just decision in the appeal.</u>

<u>78. Before adverting to the debate debated by the parties on the question of admitting the documents as additional evidence it is beneficial to notice Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Rule 2(1)(a) enjoins that the appellate Court may allow such evidence or document to be produced to get the same admitted as additional evidence if there has been improper refusal of evidence by trial Court which ought to have been admitted. Rule 2(1)(b) mandates that the appellate Court, if requires any document for pronouncement of judgment or for any other substantial cause may admit such a document as additional evidence. Clause (b) of sub-rule 1 of the rule manifests that it is only when the court "requires" it i.e. finds it needful, that additional evidence can be admitted. The word "requires" means appellate Court requires the document to enable it to pronounce judgment or for any other substantial cause. The requirement must be a genuine one and the need for additional evidence must be felt by the court itself. It is to be remembered here that power to allow additional evidence is discretionary in nature though such discretion has been circumscribed by limitations specified by provisions of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code. Judicial discretion means a discretion which is informed by tradition, methodised by analogy and disciplined by system.</u>

<u>79. The hearing of the appeal commenced on 29-10-1998 and continued on 1-11-1998, 2-11-1998, 3-11-1998 and 4-11-1998 and thereafter hearing stood adjourned to 8-11-1998. The hearing was, thereafter, held on 12-11-1998 and on that date the plaintiff-appellant filed the application it is seen that the application has been filed on a very belated stage, virtually on the conclusion of the hearing of the appeal.</u>

<u>80. It is now to be seen whether the said two documents can be admitted as additional evidence and also whether this court as the appellate Court requires the documents to enable it to give just decision in the appeal.</u>

<u>81. Clause (a) of sub-rule 1 of rule 27 is not relevant for the purpose. Clause (b) of the said sub-rule of the rule is relevant. Annexure A is a photo copy of a GD Entry registered with Motijheel Police Station dated 20-12-1984. It does not appear that the original of the GD Entry had been called for from the Motijheel Police Station and without calling for the original GD Entry from Motijheel Police Station no question arises as to the taking the document as an additional evidence under the provision of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Annexure-B is a judgment dated 17th May, 1994 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Criminal Revision No. 333 of 1988. The Revision arose out of an order passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Dhaka releasing the property from attachment and discharging the Receiver. Admittedly, the suit property remains attached in a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which was subsequently converted into a proceeding under section 146 of the Code. On a perusal of the judgment it appears that the High Court Division was of the opinion that since appeal is pending before the High Court Division and appeal being a continuation of the suit, the order of attachment and receiver would not stand vacated and discharged till the final disposal of the appeal. The High Court Division was also of the opinion that the application being under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure no second revision lay even in the garb under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Since the whole appeal is being disposed of by this judgment, the fate of attachment and receiver matter will be absolutely dependent upon the decision of the appeal and the Criminal Proceeding will be disposed of accordingly. This court does not require the documents Annexure-A and B to enable it to pronounce just decision in the appeal. The application is, accordingly, rejected.</u>

<u>82. Before parting with the matter we feel on considering a legal aspect which is a substantial question of law and also of great public interest. In this case the plaintiff Shahani Bibi did not appear before the trial Court to give testimony in support of the plaint case. It also does not appear from the record that any attempt was made to have her evidence recorded in her residence by an Advocate Commissioner appointed by the Court. No evidence and materials came forth whether she was physically unfit to come to the court to give testimony. Now the question comes whether PW 1 who is the son of the plaintiff is competent to give testimony in support of the plaint case.</u>

<u>83. Chapter IX of the Evidence Act deals with witness and who are competent witness to give testimony in any case before any court of law. Section 120 under Chapter IX of the Evidence Act enjoins that in all Civil Proceedings, the parties to the suit, and the husband or wife to the suit, shall be competent witnesses. The Golden Maxim of "Husband and Wife" who are spouses has been enshrined in this section. There is no provision in Chapter IX wherein the son has been authorized to give testimony in favour of his mother.</u>

<u>84. It now needs examination whether any person, no matter a son, daughter, or an agent on behalf of a party can be a competent witness to give testimony in a court of law. Rules 1 and 2 of Order III of the Code of Civil Procedure may conveniently be noticed in this context.</u>

<u>Rule 1 runs thus:</u>

<u>"1. Any appearance, application or act in or to any Court, required or authorized by law to be made or done by a party in such Court, may, except where otherwise expressly provided by any law for the time being in force, be made or done by the party in person, or by his recognized agent, or by a pleader appearing, applying or acting, as the case may be, on his behalf:</u>

<u>Provided that any such appearance shall, if the Court so directs, be made by the party in person."</u>

<u>Rule 2 reads thus:</u>

<u>"2. The recognized agents of parties by whom such appearances, applications and acts may be made or done are-</u>

<u>(a) persons holding powers-of-attorney, authorizing them to make and do such appearances, applications and acts on behalf of such parties;</u>

<u>(b) persons carrying on trade or business for and in the names of parties not resident within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court within which limits the appearance, application or act is made or done, in matters connected with such trade or business only, where no other agent is expressly authorized to make and do such appearances, applications and acts".</u>

<u>85. A conjoint reading of rules 1 and 2 of Order III of the Code manifests that any appearance, application or act in or to any court required or authorized by law to be made or done by a party in such court except where otherwise expressly provided by any law for the time being in force, be made or done by the party in person or by his recognized agent or by a pleader appearing, applying or acting, as the case may be, on his behalf and the recognized agent of parties by whom such appearances, applications, an act may be made or done are persons holding powers of attorney authorizing them to make or do such appearances, application and acts on behalf of such parties.</u>

<u>86. On a conspectus of the above provisions of law it clearly emerges that a person not a party to the suit or a husband or wife or an attorney got no authority to give testimony in a suit in support of the case either of the plaintiff or the defendant.</u>

<u>87. Admittedly PW 1 is not a party to the suit. Rather his mother is a party to the suit who is no other than the plaintiff. It does not also appear at all that PW 1 is an attorney on the basis of a power executed by plaintiff in his favour to give testimony on her behalf in support of the plaint case. PW 1, Md Azim, thus, was an incompetent person to give testimony on behalf of the plaintiff in support of the plaint case and the plaint case, therefore, stands disproved.</u>

88. Viewed in the perspective of the foregoing discourse and after giving our anxious consideration to all pros and cons of the case and on taking note of catena of decisions pronounced by the apex Court from time to time, the irresistible conclusion flows is, that since the plaintiff-appellant signally failed to prove her title and possession on the suit property and the defendant-respondents could successfully prove their title and possession thereon through legal evidence, plaintiffs suit was to meet the inevitable fate of dismissal and the learned trial. Judge was well justified in dismissing the suit and the judgment under challenge in this appeal having been well reasoned and well founded both on law and fact does not at all warrant any interference by us in the exercise of our appellate authority.

89. In the result, the appeal being wholly meritless, is, dismissed. The impugned judgment and decree stand maintained.

90. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case we direct the parties to bear their respective costs.
